title: Fotoni lab visit: modern physics experiments
description: Before, during and after a visit to the University of Helsinki's Fotoni laboratory: predict, plan, measure Planck's constant and e/m yourself, analyse the uncertainty and write an English lab report.

sources.title: Fotonin materiaalipankki (University of Helsinki, LUMA science education): the works, stations and group sizes
sources.note: Photoelectric effect 3 stations, e/m 2, double slit 1, Millikan (qualitative) 1, hot filament 1, spectra 3; the double-slit work is a demonstration, analysis and a report.

sources.title: Fysiikan avoin opetuslaboratorio Fotoni (University of Helsinki): upper-secondary visits, Physicum, Kumpula campus
sources.note: Upper-secondary visit: an introduction of about 15 min, lab work of about 60 min and a visit to a research department of 30–60 min; students choose the works in advance and bring laptops if possible.

sources.title: Fotoni work instruction: Valosähköinen ilmiö (short version): LEDs, vacuum tube, stopping voltage, linear fit
Fotoni work instruction: Elektronin ominaisvaraus (e/m): 100–300 V, coils N = 130, R = 0.15 m, the graph of 2U against B²r²
Fotoni work instruction: Kaksoisrakokoe: photodiode, dim green lamp, photomultiplier, 10 s counts, d = 0.3556 mm, L = 49 cm
Fotoni work instruction: Musta kappale: filament lamp at 7–10 V, prism, light sensor, temperature from the electrical power
Fotoni work instruction: Spektritutkimus: hand spectroscope, spectrometer, hydrogen, oxygen and water-vapour tubes, energy-saving lamp
Fotoni work instruction: Millikanin koe: atomiser, alpha source, about 500 V between the plates, microscope camera
Mass-to-charge ratio (Wikipedia): electron e/m = 1.75882 · 10¹¹ C/kg (CODATA), first measured by J. J. Thomson in 1897
Helmholtz coil (Wikipedia): B = (4/5)^(3/2) μ₀nI/R at the centre, coils one radius apart
Oil drop experiment (Wikipedia): Millikan and Fletcher 1909, published 1913, charges in whole multiples of e
Balmer series (Wikipedia): visible hydrogen lines 656.3, 486.1, 434.0 and 410.2 nm (in air)
Tungsten (Wikipedia): melting point 3422 °C (3695 K), so a tungsten filament's peak stays in the infrared
ITER diagnostics (iter.org): spectroscopic instruments from visible light to X-rays measure impurities and ion temperature
Planck constant (Wikipedia): exact SI value h = 6.62607015 · 10⁻³⁴ J·s since 2019
